question: How do I get my criminal record sealed or expunged, how long do I have to wait, and what does it cost?

gold_sections.why: Sealing by motion: non-conviction records (no waiting period; motion before October 1, 2027 unless the offense is on the 16-805(b) list), the 5-year (misdemeanor) and 8-year (felony) waiting periods, the excluded most-serious felonies, the interests-of-justice standard, motion contents, service on the prosecutor, waiver of waiting periods, the rule that other records' waiting periods need not be met, the 180-day ruling and 90-day sealing deadlines, and refiling after denial.

Automatic sealing of non-conviction cases and of misdemeanor convictions 10 years after the sentence, the offenses excluded from automatic sealing, and the October 1, 2027 / 90-day implementation deadlines.
Expungement by motion for non-conviction cases on the ground of actual innocence: standard of proof, filing at any time, procedure and deadlines.

Automatic expungement, convictions included, of records for decriminalized, legalized or unconstitutional offenses and pre-February 15, 2015 simple marijuana possession, by October 1, 2027 or 90 days after the case ends.

Defines 'completion of the sentence' (unconditional discharge from incarceration, probation, parole or supervised release, whichever is latest; the start of every waiting period; unpaid fines or restitution do not prevent it), 'Court' and 'Clerk'.
Court fees are not set by statute: the Superior Court may prescribe its own fees and costs.
A person may obtain his or her own arrest record to check eligibility or file a sealing or expungement motion; the District may charge a nominal fee (the only cost the statutes mention).
Effect of sealing: records removed from public view, no perjury for nondisclosure, agencies' 90-day certification, the Clerk's copies of the order and certifications, and who keeps access.
Effect of expungement: status restored as before the arrest, records limited to a nonpublic file, agencies certify within 90 days.

nuggets.text: A misdemeanor conviction can be sealed by motion once at least 5 years have passed since the sentence was completed.
nuggets.quote: For a misdemeanor offense, a waiting period of at least 5 years has elapsed since completion of the sentence

nuggets.text: A felony conviction can be sealed by motion once at least 8 years have passed since the sentence was completed.
nuggets.quote: For a felony offense, a waiting period of at least 8 years has elapsed since completion of the sentence

nuggets.text: Felonies in Offense Severity Groups 1, 2 or 3 of the Sentencing Commission's Master Grid can never be sealed.
nuggets.quote: except, that an offense in Offense Severity Group 1, 2, or 3 of the Master Grid , developed by the District of Columbia Sentencing Commission, at the time of the effective date of the Second Chance Amendment Act of 2022, passed on 2nd reading on December 20, 2022 (Enrolled version of Bill 24-63) [March 10, 2023], shall not be eligible for sealing

nuggets.text: To seal by motion, the person files a written motion and must show by a preponderance of the evidence that sealing is in the interests of justice.
nuggets.quote: files a written motion demonstrating, by a preponderance of the evidence, that it is in the interests of justice to seal the records

nuggets.quote: The Court shall grant a motion to seal pursuant to subsection (a) of this section if it is in the interests of justice to do so.

nuggets.quote: The grounds upon which eligibility for sealing is based; and (iii) Facts in support of the movant's claim

nuggets.quote: The waiting periods in subsection (a)(3)(A) of this section may be waived by the prosecutor in writing.

nuggets.quote: Issued no later than 180 days after the motion is filed, unless there exists good cause for delay.

nuggets.text: A misdemeanor conviction is sealed automatically once at least 10 years have passed since the sentence was completed, unless the offense is on the 16-805(b) exclusion list.
nuggets.quote: Citations, arrests, charges, and convictions for the commission of a misdemeanor offense that resulted in a conviction; provided, that a waiting period of at least 10 years has elapsed since completion of the sentence

nuggets.text: Automatic sealing (of both non-conviction records and misdemeanor convictions) does not apply to offenses on a statutory exclusion list, such as intrafamily offenses.
nuggets.quote: The Court shall not order automatic sealing pursuant to this section if the citation, arrest, charge, or conviction is for: (1) An intrafamily offense, as defined in § 16-1001(8)

nuggets.text: Automatically sealed misdemeanor convictions must be sealed by October 1, 2027, or within 90 days after the waiting period ends, whichever is later.
nuggets.quote: shall be sealed by October 1, 2027, or within 90 days after the expiration of the waiting period, whichever is later

nuggets.text: Expungement by motion is available for non-conviction cases on the ground of actual innocence (the offense did not occur or the person did not commit it).
nuggets.quote: The Court shall order expungement of all criminal records and court proceedings related only to citations, arrests, or charges for the commission of a criminal offense on the grounds of actual innocence

nuggets.text: Every waiting period runs from completion of the sentence: unconditional discharge from incarceration, commitment, probation, parole or supervised release, whichever is latest; unpaid fines, restitution or other court-imposed money do not prevent completion.
nuggets.quote: unconditionally discharged from incarceration, commitment, probation, parole, or supervised release, whichever is latest; provided, that nonpayment of fines, restitution, or any other monetary assessments imposed by the Court shall not prevent completion of a sentence

nuggets.text: The only cost the statutes mention: the District may charge a nominal fee for producing the person's arrest record for a sealing or expungement motion.
nuggets.quote: The District may charge the individual a nominal fee for processing this request.

nuggets.text: A case that ended without a conviction can be sealed by motion with no waiting period; for an offense not on the 16-805(b) list the motion must be filed before October 1, 2027, while for a listed offense there is no filing cutoff.
nuggets.quote: The offense is not an offense listed in § 16-805(b) and the person cited, arrested, or charged files a written motion prior to October 1, 2027; or (ii) The offense is an offense listed in § 16-805(b)

nuggets.quote: shall be expunged pursuant to subsection (a) of this section by October 1, 2027, or within 90 days after termination of the case by the prosecutor or final disposition, whichever is later

nuggets.text: An actual-innocence expungement motion can be filed at any time; there is no waiting period.
nuggets.quote: Filed at any time.

nuggets.text: No statute sets a fee for a sealing or expungement motion; the Superior Court may prescribe its own fees and costs.
nuggets.quote: The Superior Court of the District of Columbia may prescribe fees and costs

answer:
D.C. Superior Court decides these cases [N5]. Records of offenses later decriminalized or legalized, and of marijuana possession before February 15, 2015, are expunged automatically, convictions included [N17], by October 1, 2027 (or 90 days after the case ends, if later) [N18]. Non-conviction cases [N9][N21] and misdemeanor convictions 10 years after the sentence [N10][N12] are sealed automatically on a similar schedule, except listed offenses such as intrafamily offenses [N11].

You need not wait. A non-conviction case can be sealed by motion now, without waiting: file before October 1, 2027, or anytime for a listed offense [N16]. For a conviction, wait 5 years after completing a misdemeanor sentence or 8 for a felony [N1][N2], counted from unconditional discharge from prison, probation, parole or supervised release, whichever is last, even with fines unpaid [N14]. The prosecutor can waive the wait in writing [N7], and another record's unfinished wait does not block an eligible one [N22]. Felonies in Offense Severity Groups 1-3 can never be sealed [N3].

File a written motion stating your grounds and facts [N6], serve the prosecutor [N23], and show by a preponderance of the evidence that sealing serves the interests of justice [N4]; the judge must then grant it [N5], in writing within 180 days absent good cause [N8]. Expungement for actual innocence of a non-conviction charge can be sought at any time [N13][N19].

Cost: no statute sets a filing fee; the court sets its own [N20], and the District may charge a nominal arrest-record fee [N15].

gaps: No statute sets a filing fee for a motion to seal or expunge; 15-709 leaves fees and costs to the Superior Court, and the fee-waiver statute 15-712 covers only noncriminal proceedings. The arrest-record fee in 2-1402.66 is 'nominal' with no amount stated.

Requesting one's own arrest record (2-1402.66) is optional, not a statutory prerequisite for filing; it is modeled before the motion because the statute frames it as a request 'for filing a sealing or expungement motion' (a separate parallel branch does not compile to a sound net). The District's fee is a 'may', so the fee step is conditional and filing follows either way.
The statute says only that the motion 'shall be served upon the prosecutor' (passive voice); the model infers that the movant serves it.

The waiting period is modeled as an eligibility check on initial review, not as a deadline: it is the earliest time a conviction motion succeeds, and a premature motion may be dismissed without prejudice and renewed (16-806 i.5). A movant need not meet the waiting periods for every record or seek relief for every eligible record (16-806 h). The prosecutor's written waiver (16-806 e) is an eligibility input; the statute sets no procedure for requesting it.

Non-conviction records for offenses not listed in 16-805(b) can be sealed by motion only if the motion is filed before October 1, 2027 (16-806 a.1.B.i); after that they are covered by automatic sealing (16-805 a.1, c.1). Non-conviction records for listed offenses can be sealed by motion with no filing cutoff (16-806 a.1.B.ii).

The court is a black-box pool (actor kind 'court'); its review, hearing and ruling appear as messages in the movant's and agencies' processes, as in the other curated models. After initial review the court must decide whether a hearing is required (16-806 i.2.A); ordering a prosecutor response is discretionary (i.2.B), so the response and hearing steps are conditional and the path rejoins at the weighing of interests.

The Clerk must make reasonable efforts to send the order when it issues and the certifications when filed (16-807 c.3.B); the model places agency sealing after the first copy for simplicity, but the 90-day sealing and certification clocks run from the grant or order regardless of the Clerk's copy.

16-806 as downloaded includes amendments by temporary legislation that expired on September 11, 2026; the corpus does not show which words are temporary. This model avoids the likely temporary text: (i)(7) on motions dismissed between March 1, 2025 and July 14, 2025, probably the 30-day chance to amend an incomplete motion in (c)(2), and the 'unsealed and unexpunged' and 'as reasonably known to the movant' qualifiers in (c)(1)(A)(i).

Off the main path: automatic sealing (16-805) and automatic expungement (16-802) need no motion; expungement by motion on actual innocence (16-803) can be filed at any time and follows the same review, hearing and 180-day order procedure, with expungement within 90 days of the grant; fugitive-from-justice arrests (16-806 a.2, which also requires proof of appearance in the demanding jurisdiction) and misidentified arrests (16-806 g) have their own routes.

version_flags: 16-806 as downloaded 'includes amendments by temporary legislation that will expire on September 11, 2026'; those temporary amendments have expired as of 2026-10-10 and the permanent version may differ. The likely temporary text, (i)(7) (motions dismissed between March 1, 2025 and July 14, 2025), probably the 30-day amendment window in (c)(2), and possibly both the 'unsealed and unexpunged' and the 'as reasonably known to the movant' qualifiers in (c)(1)(A)(i), is not relied on here; N6 rests only on (c)(1)(A)(ii)-(iii). The permanent text may require the motion to list all of the movant's citations, arrests, charges and convictions without those qualifiers.

Automatic sealing (16-805 c) and automatic expungement (16-802 b) need only be completed by October 1, 2027 (or within 90 days after the case ends or the waiting period expires, if later), so on 2026-10-10 eligible records may not yet have been sealed or expunged automatically.
16-806(a)(1)(B)(i): a motion to seal a non-conviction record for an offense not listed in 16-805(b) must be filed before October 1, 2027; after that date such records are left to automatic sealing.
notes: D.C.'s Second Chance Amendment Act of 2022 rewrote chapter 8 of Title 16 (16-801 to 16-809): automatic expungement (16-802), expungement by motion for actual innocence (16-803), automatic sealing (16-805) and sealing by motion (16-806), all decided by the Superior Court and applied retroactively (16-808). The 16-805(b) exclusion list also covers parental kidnapping, abuse or financial exploitation of vulnerable adults, incest, misdemeanor sexual abuse and other sex offenses, registrable offenses whose registration period has not expired, dangerous crimes and crimes of violence (23-1331), and DUI, commercial-vehicle DUI and impaired driving. The prosecutor can block automatic expungement only by a written motion and clear and convincing evidence (16-802 a.2). For actual-innocence expungement the movant must prove by a preponderance that the offense did not occur or was not committed by the movant, and an acquittal or dismissal creates no presumption of innocence (16-803 a.2, e). Sealing is not erasure: sealed records stay available to courts, prosecutors, police and corrections agencies for listed purposes, and, except for fugitive arrests, to certain licensing agencies, schools and child-care facilities and some government employers to the extent they could see them before (16-807 d, 16-801 a.5), and a person need not disclose a sealed record (16-807 b). Expungement restores the person to the status before arrest (16-804 a). Victims may attend record-sealing hearings (23-1901 b.4) and the court may consider a victim's statement (16-806 b.2.B.v). Other routes kept by the savings clause (16-809): vacatur and expungement for trafficking victims (22-1844), expungement after first-offense drug-possession probation and dismissal (48-904.01 e.2), Youth Rehabilitation Act set-aside (24-906), juvenile sealing two years after discharge (16-2335) or on actual innocence (16-2335.02), and expungement for a first parental-kidnapping conviction (16-1026). Background-check providers may not report expunged, sealed or set-aside records (2-1652). The statutes state no filing fee; in practice the court's fee schedule governs, which is out of the corpus.
